name: Tweezers For Extracting Hair
description: FROM CARD: "BRASS TWEEZERS HUNG TO A ROUND BEADED CORD. THIS SPECIMEN WAS PRESENTED BY PERRI PA HOU EE AN ARAPAHO CHIEF, TO DR. F. KAUFF [sic, should be Kampf] [Las] VEGAS, N.MEX. NOTE THE TENT DESIGN ON THE TWEEZERS." "Tent design" consists of two triangles with crosses on top. Possibly could also represent a mission/church? Original list in accession file identifies as "Brass tweezers for extracting the hair. Presented by Perri-Pa-hoo-ee, a Chief of the Arapahoes, to Dr. F. Kampf, at Las Vegas, New Mexico." Rau acquired the tweezers from Kampf. Dr. F. (Ferdinand) Kampf was a civilian astronomer on the Wheeler Survey, 1873 - 1878 (his last season in the field ended in 1877).

name: Shell Scraper
description: Scraper made from a shell, cut into a square, and lashed to a folded, rough cloth, and used to remove outer layers from bast of paper mulberry. The scraper is part of a collection of kapa tools used to make barkcloth, and was made specifically for the U.S. Exploring Expedition conservation project that took place in the Department of Anthropology Conservation Lab at the Museum Support Center in 2012-2013. The scraper was made by Daniel Richard Jonathan Kapalikuokalani Maile of Kaimuki, Oahu, age 25, a Masters candidate at UH Manoa-Pacific Island Studies.

name: Paper Knife
description: During the 1890s a new style emerged that reflected naturalistic and symbolic motifs found in Japanese and other Asian design. This movement rejected the historicism that had dominated architecture and design during the previous decades and took hold across Europe and America too. In France the style was known as "Art Nouveau," after the name of the gallery belonging to its chief proponent Siegfried Bing, the Maison de L'Art Nouveau (House of the New Art). This paper knife by the American silver company George W. Shiebler & Co. typifies Art Nouveau style with its flowing lines enveloping a young woman, revered as the ideal natural beauty. The composition resolves into a pointed dagger, suggesting a tragic end to life itself. Art Nouveau reached its apex at the 1900 world's fair in Paris, which was intended to herald the new century with a new style of art. However, critics and consumers alike soon rejected Art Nouveau as too sentimental in favor of newer motifs and styles as the moment passed. By 1905 it was all but forgotten.

source_raw.did_you_know: This expressive Art Nouveau paper knife, or letter opener, was sold by the Cleveland jeweler Cowell and Hubbard around 1900.
source_raw.description: During the 1890s a new style emerged that reflected naturalistic and symbolic motifs found in Japanese and other Asian design. This movement rejected the historicism that had dominated architecture and design during the previous decades and took hold across Europe and America too. In France the style was known as "Art Nouveau," after the name of the gallery belonging to its chief proponent Siegfried Bing, the Maison de L'Art Nouveau (House of the New Art). This paper knife by the American silver company George W. Shiebler & Co. typifies Art Nouveau style with its flowing lines enveloping a young woman, revered as the ideal natural beauty. The composition resolves into a pointed dagger, suggesting a tragic end to life itself. Art Nouveau reached its apex at the 1900 world's fair in Paris, which was intended to herald the new century with a new style of art. However, critics and consumers alike soon rejected Art Nouveau as too sentimental in favor of newer motifs and styles as the moment passed. By 1905 it was all but forgotten.
